Analysis of OMICS data, practical 1

Introduction to Bash and the Linux environment

Author

Orsolya Pipek

Published

February 12, 2026

Overview

This tutorial provides a comprehensive introduction to the Linux command line and useful bash commands. You will learn essential commands for file navigation, data manipulation, and automation, which are critical skills for bioinformatics and computational biology. By the end, you’ll be able to efficiently manage large datasets, automate repetitive tasks, and build robust data analysis workflows.

1 Introduction

Welcome to this practical introduction to the Linux command line! In this tutorial, you will learn the essential bash commands and workflows needed for handling large datasets, particularly in bioinformatics and data science contexts.

1.1 What you will learn

By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

  • Navigate the Linux file system efficiently
  • Create and organize directories and files with optimal naming conventions
  • Download and manipulate large data files
  • Use powerful text processing tools
  • Automate repetitive tasks with simple loops
  • Combine commands using pipes for complex operations

1.2 Prerequisites

  • Access to a Linux terminal (via SSH to a server, WSL on Windows, or native Linux/Mac terminal)
  • A text editor (vim, nano, gedit, or any other)

1.3 How to use this tutorial

  1. Read the explanations carefully before attempting the tasks
  2. Type commands yourself rather than copy-pasting (this helps learning!)
  3. Complete each task before moving to the next section
  4. Don’t hesitate to ask for help if something is unclear
Technical note

Lines starting with $ represent the command prompt. You should type everything after the $ symbol. Output from commands will be shown without the $ prefix.

How to solve tasks

Tasks are listed at the sections they are related to and you can use the Terminal to experiment with the commands, however, for submitting your final solutions, you will need to use a Jupyter Notebook. The template notebook is available at /shared/OMICS/practical01/practical1_template.ipynb, and detailed instructions are provided in the last task (Task 25) of the tutorial.

2 Getting started: connecting to a Linux server

ssh - connect to a remote server

Before we can work with Linux commands, we need to access a Linux environment. This section covers how to connect to a remote Linux server from different operating systems.

2.1 What is SSH?

SSH (Secure Shell) is a protocol that allows you to securely connect to a remote computer over a network. When you connect via SSH, you get access to the command line of the remote server as if you were sitting right in front of it.

2.2 Connecting from different operating systems

2.2.1 Windows users

Windows users have several options for SSH connections:

2.2.1.1 Option 1: Windows Terminal with OpenSSH

Modern Windows (10 and 11) comes with OpenSSH built-in:

  1. Open Windows Terminal or PowerShell
  2. Type the SSH command:
ssh -p 2227 username@rstudio.dlab.elte.hu
  1. When prompted, enter your password (it won’t show on screen - this is normal!)

2.2.1.2 Option 2: PuTTY (classic method)

If OpenSSH doesn’t work or you prefer a graphical interface:

  1. Download and install PuTTY
  2. Open PuTTY
  3. In the Host Name field, enter: rstudio.dlab.elte.hu
  4. Set Port to 2227
  5. Click Open
  6. Enter your username and password when prompted

2.2.1.3 Option 3: MobaXterm (feature-rich alternative, recommended for Windows 10/11 for graphical interface)

For a more user-friendly experience with built-in file transfer:

  1. Download MobaXterm (free Home Edition, portable version)
  2. Unzip the portable version to a directory of your choice and run the executable file (MobaXterm_Personal_25.4.exe).
  3. Click New session → SSH
  4. Enter the remote host address (rstudio.dlab.elte.hu)
  5. Tick Specify username and enter your username in the field
  6. Change Port to 2227
  7. Under Advanced SSH settings, check if X11-Forwarding is enabled (if not, enable it)
  8. Click OK and enter your password

2.2.2 Mac users

Mac comes with a built-in terminal and SSH:

  1. Open Terminal (found in Applications → Utilities, or use Spotlight search)
  2. Type the SSH command:
ssh -p 2227 username@rstudio.dlab.elte.hu
  1. Enter your password when prompted (it won’t display - this is normal!)

2.2.3 Linux users

Linux systems have SSH pre-installed:

  1. Open your Terminal application
  2. Type the SSH command:
ssh -p 2227 username@rstudio.dlab.elte.hu
  1. Enter your password when prompted

2.3 SSH connection details

2.3.1 Basic connection command

ssh username@server.address.com

Replace:

  • username with your actual username (often your student ID)
  • server.address.com with your server’s address

2.3.2 SSH with custom port

If your server uses a non-standard port (not 22):

ssh -p 2227 username@server.address.com

The -p flag specifies the port number.

2.3.3 SSH with X11 forwarding

To run graphical applications from the server on your local screen:

ssh -X -p 2227 username@rstudio.dlab.elte.hu

The -X flag enables X11 forwarding (graphical interface forwarding).

Note on X11 forwarding
  • Linux: Works out of the box
  • Mac: Requires XQuartz to be installed
  • Windows: Requires an X server like VcXsrv or use MobaXterm which has it built-in

2.4 First time connecting

When you connect to a server for the first time, you’ll see a message like:

The authenticity of host 'server.address.com' can't be established.
ECDSA key fingerprint is SHA256:xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx.
Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no)?

Type yes and press Enter. This is normal and adds the server to your list of known hosts.

2.5 Understanding the command prompt

After logging in, you’ll see a prompt that typically looks like this:

username@hostname:~$
  • username - your username
  • hostname - the name of the computer/server (dlab-omics)
  • ~ - your current directory (~ means home directory)
  • $ - indicates you’re a regular user (# would mean root/admin)

2.6 Changing your password

Default password

For new users, the default password is test2026. You should change it to a permanent password as soon as possible.

passwd - change your password

To change your password, type passwd and press Enter. You will be asked to enter both your old (current) password and your new password twice to confirm it.

passwd

2.7 Disconnecting from the server

To close your SSH connection and return to your local machine:

exit

Or simply press Ctrl+D.

Helpful SSH tips
  • Password invisible: When typing your password, nothing appears on screen - this is a security feature, not a bug!
  • Tab completion: Press Tab to auto-complete commands and filenames
  • Command history: Use the up/down arrow keys to recall previous commands
  • Cancel command: Press Ctrl+C to stop a running command
  • Copy/Paste: In most terminals, use Ctrl+Shift+C to copy and Ctrl+Shift+V to paste (not the usual Ctrl+C/V)

3 Basic information commands

whoami - display current username
hostname - display server name
pwd - display current directory

Before diving into file operations, let’s learn some commands that tell us about our environment.

3.1 Who am I? Where am I?

3.1.1 whoami - Display current username

$ whoami
student01

This shows which user account you’re currently using.

3.1.2 hostname - Display server name

$ hostname
dlab-omics

This tells you which computer/server you’re connected to - useful when working with multiple servers!

3.1.3 pwd - Print working directory

The pwd command shows your current location in the file system.

$ pwd
/home/username

4 File system navigation

4.1 Listing files and directories: ls

ls - list files and directories

The ls command lists the contents of a directory. It has many useful options.

4.1.1 Basic listing

$ ls
Documents  Downloads  data  scripts

4.1.2 Detailed listing with file sizes

The -l flag provides a long format with detailed information:

$ ls -l
total 32
drwxr-xr-x 2 user group 4096 Jan 15 10:30 Documents
drwxr-xr-x 3 user group 4096 Jan 14 09:15 Downloads
drwxr-xr-x 5 user group 8192 Jan 16 14:22 data
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 2048 Jan 15 11:45 notes.txt

The columns show: permissions, number of links, owner, group, size (bytes), modification date/time, and name.

4.1.3 Showing hidden files

Files starting with . are hidden. Use -a to see them:

$ ls -a
.  ..  .bashrc  .profile  Documents  Downloads

4.1.4 Combining flags

Flags can be combined for more detailed output:

$ ls -la
total 48
drwxr-xr-x 6 user group 4096 Jan 16 14:30 .
drwxr-xr-x 8 root root  4096 Jan 10 08:00 ..
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group  220 Jan 10 08:00 .bash_logout
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 3526 Jan 10 08:00 .bashrc
drwxr-xr-x 2 user group 4096 Jan 15 10:30 Documents

4.1.5 Sorting by time

The -t flag sorts by modification time (newest first):

$ ls -lt

For oldest first, add -r for reverse:

$ ls -ltr

4.1.6 Human-readable file sizes

The -h flag makes file sizes human-readable (KB, MB, GB):

$ ls -lh
total 32K
drwxr-xr-x 2 user group 4.0K Jan 15 10:30 Documents
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 1.5M Jan 16 12:00 data.txt

List all files (including hidden ones) in your home directory with detailed information and human-readable sizes, sorted by modification time.

Hint

You’ll need to combine multiple flags: -a, -l, -h, and -t.

4.2 Getting help: man pages

man - get help

The man command displays the manual (documentation) for other commands.

$ man ls

This opens the full manual for the ls command. Use:

  • Space to scroll down one page
  • b to scroll up one page
  • / followed by text to search
  • q to quit
Getting help - multiple ways

Most commands support multiple ways to get help:

  • man command - Full manual page (most detailed)
  • command --help - Quick help summary
  • command -h - Short help (not all commands support this)

4.3 Visualizing directory structure: tree

tree - directory structure

The tree command displays directories in a tree-like format, making it easy to see the folder structure at a glance.

4.3.1 Basic usage

Show the directory tree starting from the current location:

$ tree
.
├── Documents
│   ├── reports
│   └── notes
├── Downloads
└── projects
    ├── analysis
    └── data

4.3.2 Show only directories (no files)

Use -d to show only directories:

$ tree -d
.
├── Documents
│   ├── reports
│   └── notes
├── Downloads
└── projects
    ├── analysis
    └── data

This is very useful for understanding your folder organization!

4.3.3 Limit depth levels

Use -L to limit how many levels deep to show:

$ tree -d -L 1
.
├── Documents
├── Downloads
└── projects

$ tree -d -L 2
.
├── Documents
│   ├── reports
│   └── notes
├── Downloads
└── projects
    ├── analysis
    └── data
When to use tree
  • Before starting a project - Understand existing folder structures
  • After creating directories - Verify your organization
  • In documentation - Show project structure to collaborators
  • During cleanup - Find empty or unnecessary directories

4.4 Changing directories: cd

cd - change directory

The cd command (change directory) allows you to navigate between directories in the file system.

4.4.1 Basic usage

Go to a specific directory:

$ cd Documents
$ pwd
/home/username/Documents

4.4.2 Go to home directory

Using cd with no arguments takes you to your home directory:

$ cd
$ pwd
/home/username

Or explicitly with ~:

$ cd ~
$ pwd
/home/username

4.4.3 Go up one directory level

Use .. to move up one level in the directory tree:

$ pwd
/home/username/projects/data
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/home/username/projects

4.4.4 Go up multiple levels

You can chain .. to go up multiple levels:

$ pwd
/home/username/projects/data/raw
$ cd ../../
$ pwd
/home/username/projects

4.4.5 Understanding paths: absolute vs. relative

Absolute path - Starts from the root directory (/):

$ cd /home/username/genomics_project/data

This works from anywhere in the file system.

Relative path - Starts from your current location:

$ pwd
/home/username/genomics_project
$ cd data/raw
$ pwd
/home/username/genomics_project/data/raw

4.4.6 Special directory symbols

  • . - Current directory
  • .. - Parent directory (one level up)
  • ~ - Home directory
  • / - Root directory (top of file system)
  • - - Previous directory

4.4.7 Go to previous directory

Use cd - to return to the previous directory:

$ pwd
/home/username/projects
$ cd /var/log
$ pwd
/var/log
$ cd -
$ pwd
/home/username/projects

This is very useful for switching between two directories!

4.4.8 Navigating with tab completion

Start typing a directory name and press Tab to auto-complete:

$ cd gen<Tab>
$ cd genomics_project/    # Auto-completed!

If multiple options exist, press Tab twice to see all possibilities.

Navigation Tips
  1. Use tab completion - Saves time and prevents typos
  2. Use cd - - Quick way to toggle between two directories
  3. Use ~ - Quick way to reference home directory from anywhere
  4. Combine with ls - Use ls to see where you can go before using cd
Task 4

  1. Use pwd to see your current location

5 Creating and organizing: directories and files

5.1 Creating empty files: touch

touch - create empty file

The touch command creates an empty file or updates the timestamp (last modification time) of an existing file.

$ touch newfile.txt

This is useful for creating placeholder files or testing purposes.

$ touch file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt

You can create multiple files at once!

5.2 Creating directories: mkdir

mkdir - create directory

Good directory structure is essential for managing large datasets. Use mkdir to create new directories.

$ mkdir my_project

Create multiple directories at once:

$ mkdir data scripts results

Create nested directories with -p:

$ mkdir -p project/data/raw

5.3 Optimal folder and file naming conventions

Best practices for naming
  1. Use descriptive names: patient_samples.txt not data.txt
  2. Avoid spaces: Use underscores _ or hyphens - instead
    • Good: genome_assembly.fasta
    • Bad: genome assembly.fasta
  3. Use lowercase: Easier to type and less error-prone
  4. Include dates: Use ISO format YYYY-MM-DD
    • Example: 2024-01-15_experiment_results.csv
  5. Version numbers: Use v1, v2 or semantic versioning
    • Example: analysis_v2.3_final.R
  6. Be consistent: Pick a convention and stick to it
Task 5

Create a directory structure for a genomics project with the following layout:

genomics_project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
├── scripts/
├── results/
└── documentation/
  1. Use a single command to create all directories at once.
  2. Use another command to check if the directories were created correctly.
Hint

You can create all directories in one command by listing them all, or use -p to create parent directories as needed.

5.4 Moving and renaming files: mv

mv - move/rename

The mv command moves files or directories to a new location, or renames them.

5.4.1 Renaming a file

$ mv oldname.txt newname.txt

This renames oldname.txt to newname.txt in the same directory.

5.4.2 Renaming a directory

$ mv old_folder new_folder

5.4.3 Moving a file to a different directory

$ mv file.txt /path/to/destination/

5.4.4 Moving and renaming simultaneously

$ mv data.txt results/analysis_data.txt

This moves data.txt to the results directory and renames it to analysis_data.txt.

5.4.5 Moving multiple files

$ mv file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt destination_folder/

The last argument must be a directory when moving multiple files.

5.4.6 Moving with wildcards

$ mv *.txt text_files/

This moves all .txt files to the text_files directory.

Warning!

mv will overwrite files without warning if a file with the same name already exists in the destination! Use -i for interactive mode to ask before overwriting:

$ mv -i oldfile.txt newfile.txt

5.5 Copying files: cp

cp - copy

The cp command copies files or directories.

5.5.1 Copy a file

$ cp source.txt destination.txt

This creates a copy of source.txt called destination.txt.

5.5.2 Copy to a different directory

$ cp file.txt /path/to/destination/

5.5.3 Copy and rename

$ cp original.txt backup/original_backup.txt

5.5.4 Copy multiple files

$ cp file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt destination_folder/

5.5.5 Copy directories: -r

Use -r (recursive) to copy entire directories:

$ cp -r source_folder/ destination_folder/

This copies the entire source_folder and all its contents.

5.5.6 Preserve attributes: -p

Use -p to preserve timestamps, permissions, and ownership:

$ cp -p important_file.txt backup_file.txt

5.5.7 Interactive mode: -i

Ask before overwriting:

$ cp -i file.txt existing_file.txt

5.5.8 Combining options

$ cp -rp original_project/ backup_project/

This recursively copies a directory while preserving all attributes.

cp vs mv
  • cp creates a duplicate, original file remains
  • mv moves the file, original location is emptied
  • Both can rename files

5.6 Removing files and directories: rm

rm - delete

The rm command deletes files and directories.

CRITICAL WARNING!

rm is PERMANENT - there is no trash/recycle bin in Linux! Deleted files cannot be recovered. Always double-check before using rm, especially with wildcards or on important data!

5.6.1 Remove a file

$ rm unwanted_file.txt

5.6.2 Remove multiple files

$ rm file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt

5.6.3 Remove with wildcards

$ rm *.tmp

This removes all files ending in .tmp.

5.6.4 Interactive mode: -i

Ask for confirmation before each deletion:

$ rm -i file.txt

This is highly recommended when you’re learning!

5.6.5 Remove directories: -r

Use -r (recursive) to remove directories and their contents:

$ rm -r folder_name/

5.6.6 Force removal: -f

Force removal without prompts (use with extreme caution!):

$ rm -f file.txt

5.6.7 Combining options

$ rm -rf folder/    # Remove folder and contents without asking
NEVER do this! 
$ rm -rf /    # NEVER RUN THIS! Deletes everything on the system!
$ rm -rf /*   # NEVER RUN THIS EITHER!

These commands would destroy your entire system. Always be careful with rm -rf and wildcards!

5.6.8 Safer alternative: rmdir

rmdir - remove directory

For empty directories, use rmdir instead:

$ rmdir empty_folder/

rmdir only works on empty directories, which prevents accidental deletion of important data.

5.7 Practical examples combining mv, cp, and rm

5.7.1 Create a backup before modifying

$ cp important_data.txt important_data_backup.txt
# Now safely edit important_data.txt

5.7.2 Organize files

$ mkdir archive
$ mv old_*.txt archive/
$ cp config.txt archive/config_backup.txt

5.7.3 Clean up after processing

$ cp results.txt final_results.txt
$ rm intermediate_*.txt
$ mv final_results.txt results/

6 Symbolic links

ln - symbolic link

6.1 What are symbolic links?

A symbolic link (symlink) is like a shortcut or pointer to another file or directory. Instead of copying a large file multiple times, you can create links that point to the original file. This saves disk space!

6.2 Creating symbolic links: ln -s

$ ln -s /path/to/original/file.txt link_name.txt

This creates a link called link_name.txt that points to the original file.

6.2.1 Practical example

$ ln -s /data/reference/hg38.fa reference_genome.fa

Now reference_genome.fa points to the large reference genome file without copying it!

6.2.2 Creating links to directories

$ ln -s /shared/databases/ my_databases

You can link to entire directories too!

6.3 Checking links

When you list files with ls -l, symbolic links show where they point:

$ ls -l
lrwxrwxrwx 1 user group   24 Jan 15 10:30 reference_genome.fa -> /data/reference/hg38.fa
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 1.5M Jan 16 12:00 data.txt

The l at the beginning indicates it’s a link, and the -> shows the target.

6.4 Removing symbolic links: unlink

unlink - remove symbolic link

$ unlink link_name.txt

Or you can use rm:

$ rm link_name.txt
Important!
  • Removing a link does NOT delete the original file
  • If you delete the original file, the link becomes broken
  • Links take almost no disk space (just a few bytes)

7 Downloading files: wget

wget - download

The wget command downloads files from the internet. This is particularly useful for obtaining public datasets.

7.1 Basic download

$ wget https://example.com/data/sample.txt

7.2 Download with a custom name

Use -O (capital O) to specify the output filename:

$ wget -O my_file.txt https://example.com/data/sample.txt

7.3 Download to a specific directory

$ wget -P data/raw/ https://example.com/data/sample.txt

7.4 Continue interrupted downloads

Use -c to continue a partially downloaded file:

$ wget -c https://example.com/large_file.gz

8 File permissions and protection

8.1 Understanding file permissions

In Linux, every file and directory has permissions that control who can read, write, or execute them. This is crucial for:

  • Protecting raw data from accidental deletion
  • Collaborating safely on shared servers
  • Maintaining data integrity

8.2 Viewing permissions with ls -l

$ ls -l
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 1024 Jan 15 10:30 data.txt
drwxr-xr-x 2 user group 4096 Jan 15 10:31 results

The first column shows permissions (e.g., -rw-r--r-- or drwxr-xr-x):

-rw-r--r--
│││││││││└─ Others: execute (-)
││││││││└── Others: write (-)
│││││││└─── Others: read (r)
││││││└──── Group: execute (-)
│││││└───── Group: write (-)
││││└────── Group: read (r)
│││└─────── Owner (you): execute (-)
││└──────── Owner (you): write (w)
│└───────── Owner (you): read (r)
└────────── File type: - (file) or d (directory) or l (link)

8.3 Permission types

  • r (read) - Can view the file contents or list directory contents
  • w (write) - Can modify the file or add/remove files in a directory
  • x (execute) - Can run the file as a program or enter the directory

8.4 Changing permissions: chmod

chmod - change permissions

The chmod command changes file permissions.

8.4.1 Adding permissions

$ chmod u+w filename.txt    # Add write permission for user (owner = you)
$ chmod u+r filename.txt    # Add read permission for user (owner = you)
$ chmod u+x script.sh       # Add execute permission for user (owner = you)

8.4.2 Removing permissions

$ chmod u-w filename.txt    # Remove write permission for user
$ chmod u-r filename.txt    # Remove read permission for user
$ chmod u-x script.sh       # Remove execute permission for user

8.4.3 Permission targets

  • u - User (owner)
  • g - Group (group you are a member of)
  • o - Others
  • a - All (user, group, and others)

8.4.4 Recursive changes

Use -R to change permissions for directories and all their contents:

$ chmod -R u+w my_directory/     # give write permission to the owner (you) for all files and directories in the my_directory directory

8.5 Protecting raw data

Best practice: make raw data read-only!

Once you download or receive raw data, immediately make it read-only to prevent accidental deletion or modification:

$ chmod -R u-w RAW_DATA/

This removes write permissions, protecting your data from accidents!

8.5.1 When you need to modify protected files

If you need to uncompress or modify a read-only file:

  1. Temporarily add write permissions
  2. Perform the operation
  3. Remove write permissions again
$ chmod u+w file.gz         # Add write permission
$ gunzip file.gz            # Uncompress (see below for more details)
$ chmod u-w file            # Remove write permission again

8.6 Checking disk space

df - disk free space

du - disk usage

Before working with large files, check available space:

8.6.1 df - Disk Free space

$ df -h
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1       100G   45G   50G  47% /

The -h flag shows human-readable sizes (GB, MB instead of bytes).

8.6.2 du - Disk Usage

$ du -h file.txt            # Size of a single file
$ du -sh directory/         # Total size of a directory
$ du -h --max-depth=1       # Size of immediate subdirectories

9 Working with compressed files

gunzip - decompress

gzip - compress

9.1 Decompressing files: gunzip

Many bioinformatics files are compressed with gzip to save space. These files end with .gz.

$ gunzip chr22_reference.fa.gz

This will decompress the file and remove the .gz extension.

To keep the original compressed file, use -k:

$ gunzip -k chr22_reference.fa.gz
Warning

Decompressing large genome files can take significant disk space. Always check available space with df -h before decompressing.

Task 10
  1. Decompress the file you downloaded previously (chr22_reference.fa.gz), but keep the original compressed version.
  2. Compare the file size of the decompressed file with the original compressed file.

9.2 Creating and extracting archives: tar

tar - create and extract archives

The tar command creates archive files (like .zip files in Windows). Archives bundle multiple files/directories into a single file, often with compression.

9.2.1 Creating a compressed archive

$ tar -czvf archive_name.tar.gz directory_to_archive/

Options explained:

  • -c - Create an archive
  • -z - Compress with gzip
  • -v - Verbose (show progress, write information to the terminal)
  • -f - Filename follows

9.2.2 Creating an archive of multiple items

$ tar -czvf my_data.tar.gz folder1/ folder2/ file1.txt file2.txt

9.2.3 Extracting a compressed archive

$ tar -xzvf archive_name.tar.gz

Options:

  • -x - Extract the archive
  • -z - Decompress (gzip)
  • -v - Verbose
  • -f - Filename follows

9.2.4 Extracting to a specific directory

$ tar -xzvf archive_name.tar.gz -C /path/to/destination/

9.2.5 Viewing archive contents without extracting

$ tar -tzvf archive_name.tar.gz

The -t option lists contents without extracting.

Common archive extensions
  • .tar.gz or .tgz - tar archive compressed with gzip (most common in bioinformatics)
  • .tar.bz2 - tar archive compressed with bzip2 (better compression, slower)
  • .tar - uncompressed tar archive
  • .zip - use unzip command instead of tar

10 Viewing file contents

cat - display entire file

zcat - view compressed file

head - view first lines

tail - view last lines

less - view contents page by page

more - view contents page by page

zless - view compressed contents page by page

10.1 Viewing entire files: cat

The cat command displays the entire contents of a file.

$ cat small_file.txt

For compressed files without decompressing, use zcat:

$ zcat file.txt.gz
Note

cat is short for concatenate - it can also combine multiple files, which we’ll see later.

Warning: Don’t cat large files!

Never use cat on large files (like genome files) - it will flood your terminal! Use less or head instead, see below.

10.2 Viewing the beginning: head

The head command shows the first 10 lines of a file by default.

$ head genomic_data.txt

Specify a different number of lines with -n:

$ head -n 20 genomic_data.txt

Or use the shorthand:

$ head -20 genomic_data.txt

10.3 Viewing the end: tail

The tail command shows the last 10 lines by default.

$ tail genomic_data.txt

Show the last 15 lines:

$ tail -n 15 genomic_data.txt

10.4 Interactive file viewers: less and more

For large files, use less or more to view them page by page without loading the entire file into memory.

10.4.1 less - The better viewer (recommended)

$ less large_file.txt

Navigation in less:

  • Space or Page Down - Next page
  • b or Page Up - Previous page
  • Arrow keys - Move up/down one line
  • g - Go to beginning of file
  • G - Go to end of file
  • / - Search forward (type search term, press Enter)
  • ? - Search backward
  • n - Next search result
  • N - Previous search result
  • q - Quit

10.4.2 more - Simpler viewer

$ more large_file.txt

Navigation in more:

  • Space - Next page
  • Enter - Next line
  • q - Quit
less vs more

less is more powerful than more:

  • less can scroll both forward AND backward
  • more can only scroll forward
  • less has better search functionality
  • Despite the name, less is more!

10.4.3 Viewing compressed files with less

$ zless file.txt.gz

This lets you view compressed files without decompressing them first!

10.5 Counting lines: wc

wc - count (lines, words, characters)

The wc command counts lines, words, and characters.

Count lines with -l:

$ wc -l genomic_data.txt
1000 genomic_data.txt

Count words with -w:

$ wc -w genomic_data.txt

Count characters with -c:

$ wc -c genomic_data.txt

11 Searching and filtering: grep

grep - search & filter

The grep command searches for patterns in files. It’s incredibly powerful for filtering large datasets.

11.1 Basic search

Search for a specific word or pattern:

$ grep "ATCG" sequences.txt

11.2 Case-insensitive search

Use -i to ignore case:

$ grep -i "gene" annotations.txt

11.3 Show line numbers

Use -n to show line numbers:

$ grep -n "mutation" variants.txt

11.4 Count matches

Use -c to count matching lines:

$ grep -c ">" sequences.fasta

11.5 Invert match

Use -v to show lines that DON’T match:

$ grep -v "#" data.vcf

This is very useful for filtering out comment lines!

11.6 Regular expressions with grep

11.6.1 Lines starting with a pattern

Use ^ to match the beginning of a line:

$ grep "^>" sequences.fasta

This finds all FASTA headers (lines starting with >).

11.6.2 Lines ending with a pattern

Use $ to match the end of a line:

$ grep "complete$" annotations.txt

11.6.3 Finding comment lines

Most bioinformatics files use # for comments at the beginning of the line:

$ grep "^#" data.vcf

12 Getting help and version information

12.1 Getting help: -h or –help

Most commands provide help documentation:

$ grep --help
$ ls --help

Some programs use -h:

$ wget -h

12.2 Checking versions

It’s important to document which version of tools you’re using:

$ grep --version
$ wget --version

Some bioinformatics tools use different flags:

$ samtools --version
$ bwa

13 Useful commands for workflows

13.1 The echo command

echo - display text

The echo command prints text to the screen or to a file.

13.1.1 Basic usage

$ echo "Hello World"
Hello World

13.1.2 Echo with special characters: -e

The -e flag allows interpretation of escape sequences:

$ echo -e "Line 1\nLine 2\nLine 3"
Line 1
Line 2
Line 3

Common escape sequences:

  • \n - Newline
  • \t - Tab
  • \\ - Backslash

13.1.3 Creating multi-line files

$ echo -e "sample1\nsample2\nsample3" > samples.txt

This creates a file with three lines!

13.1.4 Tabs in output

$ echo -e "Name\tAge\tCity"
Name    Age    City

$ echo -e "Alice\t25\tBoston\nBob\t30\tNew York" > people.txt

13.1.5 Echo without newline: -n

The -n flag suppresses the trailing newline:

$ echo -n "Processing..."
$ echo " Done!"
Processing... Done!

13.1.6 Redirecting output

> - redirect output to a file (overwrites if exists)

>> - append output to a file

Create or append to files:

$ echo "First line" > file.txt      # Creates or overwrites
$ echo "Second line" >> file.txt    # Appends
$ echo "Third line" >> file.txt     # Appends
Redirection Operators
  • > - Redirects output to a file (overwrites if exists)
  • >> - Appends output to a file
  • These work with any command, not just echo!

13.2 The date command

date - display date and time

The date command displays the current date and time.

13.2.1 Basic usage

$ date
Thu Jan 22 14:30:45 UTC 2026

13.2.2 Custom formats

Use format specifiers with +:

$ date +%Y-%m-%d
2026-01-22

$ date +%Y%m%d
20260122

$ date +"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"
2026-01-22 14:30:45

Common format codes:

  • %Y - Year (4 digits)
  • %m - Month (01-12)
  • %d - Day (01-31)
  • %H - Hour (00-23)
  • %M - Minute (00-59)
  • %S - Second (00-59)

13.2.3 Using date in filenames

$ touch analysis_$(date +%Y%m%d).log
$ ls
analysis_20260122.log

$ tar -czvf backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz my_data/

This creates timestamped files automatically!

13.2.4 Using date for versioning

$ cp script.sh script_$(date +%Y%m%d).sh
Best Practice: Date-based Versioning

Always include dates in your filenames:

  • Scripts: analysis_20260122.sh or analysis_v20260122.sh
  • Results: results_20260122.txt
  • Logs: log_20260122.log

Use ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD) for proper sorting!

14 Working with variables

14.1 Referencing variables with $

Variables store values that can be reused. Reference them with $.

14.1.1 Setting a variable

$ PROJECT_DIR="/home/user/genomics_project"
$ SAMPLE_NAME="patient_001"
Important

No spaces around the = sign!

14.1.2 Using variables

$ echo $PROJECT_DIR
/home/user/genomics_project

$ ls $PROJECT_DIR/data/

$ cd $PROJECT_DIR

14.1.3 Variables in file paths

$ REFERENCE_DIR="/data/references"
$ REFERENCE_FILE="hg38.fa"

$ ls $REFERENCE_DIR/$REFERENCE_FILE

15 Transferring files: scp

scp - secure copy

rsync - secure copy

15.1 Copying files between computers

When working with remote servers, you often need to transfer files between your local computer and the server. The scp (secure copy) command does this securely.

15.2 Basic SCP syntax

15.2.1 Copy FROM server TO your local machine

$ scp username@server.address.com:/path/to/remote/file.txt /local/destination/

15.2.2 Copy FROM your local machine TO server

$ scp /local/file.txt username@server.address.com:/path/to/remote/destination/

15.3 Copying directories: -r

Use -r for recursive copy (entire directories):

$ scp -r username@server.address.com:/path/to/remote/folder/ /local/destination/

$ scp -r /local/folder/ username@server.address.com:/path/to/remote/destination/

15.4 Practical examples

15.4.1 Download results from server

$ scp -r username@server.address.com:/home/username/results/ ~/Downloads/

15.4.2 Upload a script to server

$ scp analysis.sh username@server.address.com:/home/username/scripts/

15.4.3 Copy with custom port

If your server uses a non-standard SSH port:

$ scp -P 2227 file.txt username@server.address.com:/destination/

Note: scp uses -P (capital P) for port, while ssh uses -p (lowercase)!

Alternative: rsync

For large transfers or resuming interrupted transfers, consider using rsync:

$ rsync -avz -e ssh /local/folder/ username@server:/remote/folder/
Note

You must run scp from your local machine in a separate terminal window (not while connected to the server via SSH). Or you can transfer from server to server if you have access to both.

Note

Alternatively, if you are using MobaXterm, you can use its File Manager to transfer files between your local machine and the server via a GUI (click on Download or Upload).

16 Combining commands: pipes

| - pipe output

16.1 The power of piping: |

The pipe | sends the output of one command as input to another. This is one of the most powerful features of the command line!

16.1.1 Basic example

Get the first line of the last 5 lines:

$ tail -5 data.txt | head -1

16.1.2 Practical examples

Count FASTA sequences:

$ grep "^>" sequences.fasta | wc -l

Find and count specific patterns:

$ grep "mutation" variants.txt | grep -v "silent" | wc -l

Sort and show unique entries:

$ cat sample_names.txt | sort | uniq     # see below for more details

16.1.3 More complex pipes

$ cat annotations.gff | grep -v "^#" | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c     # see below for more details

This pipeline:

  1. Displays the file
  2. Removes comment lines
  3. Extracts the 3rd column
  4. Sorts the entries
  5. Counts unique entries

17 File manipulation

sort - sort

uniq - unique

cat - concatenate

cut - extract columns

paste - merge files

17.1 Sorting files: sort

Sort lines alphabetically:

$ sort genes.txt

Sort numerically with -n:

$ sort -n numbers.txt

Reverse sort with -r:

$ sort -r genes.txt

Sort by a specific column (tab-delimited files):

$ sort -k2 -n data.tsv

This sorts by the 2nd column numerically.

17.2 Concatenating files

Combine multiple files vertically:

$ cat file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt > combined.txt

Combine files with headers (keeping only one header):

$ head -1 file1.txt > combined.txt
$ tail -n +2 file1.txt >> combined.txt
$ tail -n +2 file2.txt >> combined.txt
Note
  • > creates a new file (or overwrites existing)
  • >> appends to a file

17.3 Extracting columns: cut

The cut command extracts specific columns from tab-delimited or other structured files.

17.3.1 Extract specific columns (tab-delimited)

$ cut -f1 data.tsv              # Extract column 1
$ cut -f1,3 data.tsv            # Extract columns 1 and 3
$ cut -f1-3 data.tsv            # Extract columns 1 through 3

17.3.2 Using different delimiters

For comma-separated files (CSV):

$ cut -d',' -f2 data.csv        # Extract column 2, comma-delimited

For space-delimited files:

$ cut -d' ' -f1,2 data.txt      # Extract columns 1 and 2, space-delimited

17.3.3 Practical example

Extract chromosome and position from a BED file:

$ cut -f1,2 genes.bed
chr1    12345
chr1    67890
chr2    11111

17.4 Merging files side-by-side: paste

The paste command merges files column-wise (side by side).

17.4.1 Basic paste

$ paste file1.txt file2.txt

If file1.txt contains:

A
B
C

And file2.txt contains:

1
2
3

The output will be:

A    1
B    2
C    3

17.4.2 Custom delimiter

By default, paste uses tabs. Change with -d:

$ paste -d',' file1.txt file2.txt
A,1
B,2
C,3

17.4.3 Paste multiple files

$ paste genes.txt positions.txt scores.txt > combined.txt
Common delimiters
  • Tab: \t (default for paste)
  • Comma: ,
  • Semicolon: ;
  • Space:
  • Pipe: |

Tab and comma are most common in bioinformatics!

17.5 Removing duplicates: uniq

The uniq command filters adjacent duplicate lines.

Important!

uniq only removes adjacent duplicates. Always sort first!

17.5.1 Basic usage

$ sort data.txt | uniq

17.5.2 Count occurrences

$ sort data.txt | uniq -c
   3 apple
   2 banana
   1 cherry

The -c flag counts how many times each line appears.

17.5.3 Show only duplicates

$ sort data.txt | uniq -d

17.5.4 Show only unique lines (no duplicates)

$ sort data.txt | uniq -u

17.6 Practical examples combining tools

17.6.1 Count unique values in a column

$ cut -f1 genes.bed | sort | uniq -c
  150 chr1
   89 chr2
   67 chr3

17.6.2 Extract and count gene names

$ cut -f4 genes.gtf | sort | uniq | wc -l

17.6.3 Create summary statistics

$ cut -f1 variants.vcf | grep -v "^#" | sort | uniq -c

This counts variants per chromosome!

    chr1    100    GeneA
chr1    200    GeneB
chr2    150    GeneC

chr1    400    GeneB

  3. Count how many times each chromosome appears (use sort and uniq -c).

18 Automation with loops

for; do; done - loop

18.1 Basic for loop syntax

Loops allow you to repeat commands for multiple items.

18.1.1 Simple loop

$ for i in 1 2 3 4 5
do
  echo "Processing item $i"
done

18.1.2 Loop over files

$ for file in *.txt
do
  echo "Processing $file"
  wc -l $file
done

18.1.3 Loop with command substitution

$ for sample in sample1 sample2 sample3
do
  echo "Analyzing $sample"
  grep ">" ${sample}.fasta | wc -l
done

18.1.4 One-line loop

Loops can be written on one line using ;:

$ for file in *.txt; do wc -l $file; done

18.2 Practical example: renaming files

$ for file in *.txt
do
  mv $file ${file%.txt}_processed.txt
done

This adds _processed before the .txt extension.

Task 22

Create a loop that:

  1. Processes all .txt files in your current directory.
  2. For each file, prints the filename and the number of lines it contains.
  3. Saves this information to a file called file_summary.txt
Hint

You can redirect the output of the entire loop using done > output_file.txt

19 Splitting and organizing data

awk - pattern scanning and processing

19.1 Splitting files by column values

Often you need to split a large file into multiple files based on a column value (e.g., by chromosome).

19.1.1 Using awk to split by first column

Create a simple example file:

$ cat > example_data.txt << 'EOF'
chr1    gene1   100
chr1    gene2   150
chr2    gene3   200
chr2    gene4   250
chr3    gene5   300
EOF

Split by chromosome:

$ awk '{print > "chromosome_"$1".txt"}' example_data.txt

This creates separate files for each chromosome: chromosome_chr1.txt, chromosome_chr2.txt, etc.

19.1.2 More controlled splitting

$ for chr in chr1 chr2 chr3
do
  grep "^$chr" example_data.txt > ${chr}_data.txt
done

Create a tab-delimited file with data from at least 3 different chromosomes (chr1, chr2, chr3), then split it into separate files for each chromosome. Make sure that the resulting files contain lines in an ascending order based on the position column. Use | for piping commands.

20 Running graphical applications from SSH

firefox & - open browser

igv & - genome viewer

jupyter notebook - start notebook

When connected to a remote server via SSH with X11 forwarding enabled (ssh -X), you can launch graphical applications that will display on your local computer. This is incredibly useful for bioinformatics tools with graphical interfaces.

Prerequisites
  • SSH with X11 forwarding: Connect using ssh -X username@server.address.com
  • X Server on your local machine:
    • Windows (MobaXterm): Built-in X server (starts automatically)
    • Mac: Install XQuartz
    • Linux: X server already installed

20.1 Direct launch (if X11 configured)

20.1.1 Example 1: Firefox Web Browser

Launch Firefox from the remote server:

$ firefox &

The & at the end runs the program in the background, so you can continue using the terminal.

Firefox will open in a new window on your local screen, but it’s actually running on the remote server!

Tip

If Firefox is slow to start, be patient - it’s loading over the network. You can check if it’s running with ps aux | grep firefox

20.1.2 Example 2: IGV (Integrative Genomics Viewer)

IGV is a popular tool for visualizing genomic data, which you will use during the next practicals:

$ igv &

The IGV graphical interface will appear on your screen, allowing you to:

  • Load reference genomes
  • View BAM files
  • Visualize variant calls
  • Explore genomic regions interactively

20.1.3 Example 3: Jupyter Notebook

Jupyter Notebook provides an interactive environment for data analysis, which you will also encounter during some of the practicals.

$ jupyter notebook

This will:

  1. Start the Jupyter server on the remote machine
  2. Attempt to open a browser window
  3. Display a URL with a token (e.g., http://localhost:8888/?token=...)
Task 24

Practice launching graphical applications:

  1. Connect to your server with X11 forwarding: ssh -X -p 2227 username@rstudio.dlab.elte.hu
  2. Verify X11 is working: echo $DISPLAY
  3. Launch these applications one by one:
    • firefox
    • igv &
    • jupyter notebook (using port forwarding method if preferred)
  4. Take a screenshot showing the graphical application window running
  5. Submit your screenshot as proof of successful X11 forwarding

Important: The screenshot should show:

  • The application window (Firefox, IGV, and/or Jupyter)
  • Proof it’s running from the remote server (e.g., terminal in background showing the ssh session)

20.2 Method 2: Port forwarding (recommended for Jupyter)

For better performance, use SSH port forwarding instead of X11:

  1. Connect with port forwarding:
$ ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888 -p 2227 username@rstudio.dlab.elte.hu
  1. Start Jupyter on the server:
$ jupyter notebook --no-browser

  1. Copy the URL shown in the terminal (looks like http://localhost:8888/?token=abc123...)

  2. Paste it into your local browser (Firefox, Chrome, etc. on your own computer)

Understanding Port Forwarding

The -L 8888:localhost:8888 flag creates a tunnel that forwards port 8888 on your local machine to port 8888 on the remote server. This is more efficient than X11 forwarding for web-based applications.

20.3 Checking if X11 Forwarding is Working

Before launching graphical applications, verify X11 is working:

$ echo $DISPLAY
localhost:11.0

If you see output like localhost:11.0 or similar, X11 forwarding is active!

If it’s empty, reconnect with the -X flag:

$ ssh -X -p 2227 username@rstudio.dlab.elte.hu

20.4 Common issues and solutions

20.4.1 Error: Can’t open display

Problem: X11 forwarding is not enabled

Solution:

# Reconnect with X11 forwarding
$ ssh -X -p 2227 username@rstudio.dlab.elte.hu

# Check DISPLAY variable is set
$ echo $DISPLAY

20.4.2 Application opens but is very slow

Problem: Graphical data being sent over network

Solutions:

  • Use a wired connection instead of WiFi
  • For web apps like Jupyter, use port forwarding instead
  • Close unnecessary graphical elements
  • Use command-line alternatives when possible

20.4.3 command not found

Problem: Software not installed or not in PATH

Solution:

# Check if the program exists
$ which firefox
$ which igv

21 Working with Jupyter Notebooks

Jupyter Notebook is an interactive environment that combines code, text, and visualizations in a single document. It’s widely used in data science and bioinformatics for documenting analyses, running code interactively, and sharing results.

21.1 What is a Jupyter Notebook?

A Jupyter Notebook consists of:

  • Cells - individual blocks that contain either code or text
  • Kernel - the computational engine (e.g., Python, R, Bash)
  • Output - results displayed directly below code cells
  • Markdown - formatted text for documentation

Notebooks are saved as .ipynb files (IPython Notebook format).

Jupyter Notebooks are a powerful tool for:

  • Documenting your workflow with Markdown
  • Running code interactively and seeing immediate results
  • Combining bash commands with data analysis
  • Creating reproducible analyses that others can follow
  • Sharing your work as a single, self-contained file

21.2 Launching Jupyter Notebook

As covered in the previous section, either use X11 forwarding or port forwarding to launch Jupyter. See the Running graphical applications from SSH section for more details.

21.3 Creating your first notebook

21.3.1 Step 1: Navigate to your working directory

In the Jupyter interface, navigate to your home directory and create a folder for this practical:

  1. Click New → Folder (on the right side of the interface)
  2. Select the new folder by checking the box next to it
  3. Click Rename and name it practical1
  4. Click on the practical1 folder to enter it

21.3.2 Step 2: Create a new notebook

  1. Inside the practical1 folder, click New → Genomics Environment
  2. A new notebook will open in a new browser tab, named Untitled.ipynb.
Notebook interface

The notebook interface shows:

  • Menu bar at the top (File, Edit, View, etc.)
  • Toolbar with common actions (save, add cell, run, etc.)
  • Cells in the main area
  • Kernel indicator in the top-right corner

21.3.3 Step 3: Save and rename your notebook

  1. Click on the notebook name Untitled at the top (next to the Jupyter logo)
  2. Type a new name: tasks1
  3. Click Rename

The notebook is automatically saved as tasks1.ipynb in your practical1 folder.

Auto-save

Jupyter notebooks auto-save periodically, but it’s good practice to manually save frequently using:

  • Ctrl+S (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+S (Mac)
  • Or click the save icon (💾) in the toolbar

21.4 Selecting a kernel

The kernel is the computational engine that executes your code. Different kernels support different programming languages.

21.4.1 Checking Current Kernel

Look at the top-right corner of the notebook - it shows the current kernel (e.g., Genomics Environment).

21.4.2 Changing the Kernel

If you need to change kernels, because you want to use either a different programming language or a different set of tools:

  1. Click Kernel in the menu bar
  2. Select Change kernel
  3. Choose from available kernels (Genomics Environment, Python, etc.)

For this and our following practicals, we’ll use the Genomics Environment kernel, which is a custom kernel with a Python base and additional tools for bioinformatics. Bash commands (detailed above) can be run in Jupyter Notebook code cells by using the ! prefix (see below).

21.5 Working with cells

Jupyter notebooks contain two main types of cells:

21.5.1 1. Code Cells

Code cells contain executable code. By default, new cells are code cells.

To run a code cell:

  • Click the cell and press Shift+Enter (runs cell and moves to next)
  • Or press Ctrl+Enter (runs cell and stays in current cell)
  • Or click the Run button (▶) in the toolbar

Example - Python code:

# This is a Python code cell
print("Hello from Jupyter!")
x = 5 + 3
print(f"5 + 3 = {x}")

Output:

Hello from Jupyter!
5 + 3 = 8

21.5.2 2. Markdown Cells

Markdown cells contain formatted text for documentation, explanations, and notes.

To create a Markdown cell:

  1. Click on a cell
  2. Change it to Markdown using:
    • Dropdown menu in toolbar: Code → Markdown
    • Or press Esc then M (keyboard shortcut)

To edit a Markdown cell:

  • Double-click the cell (or press Enter when selected)
  • Type your markdown content
  • Press Shift+Enter to render it

Example - Markdown syntax:

# This is a Heading 1
## This is a Heading 2

This is regular text with **bold** and *italic* formatting.

- Bullet point 1
- Bullet point 2

1. Numbered item
2. Another item

`inline code` looks like this
```bash
# Code blocks look like this
ls -la
```

Markdown Cheat Sheet

Common Markdown syntax:

  • # Heading - Creates headings (use #, ##, ###, etc.)
  • **bold** - Bold text
  • *italic* - Italic text
  • `code` - Inline code
  • - item - Bullet points
  • 1. item - Numbered lists
  • ```language ``` - Code blocks
  • [link](https://example.com) - Links
  • ![alt text](image.png) - Images

21.6 Running bash commands in Jupyter

Even when using a Python kernel, you can run bash/terminal commands in Jupyter by prefixing them with !

21.6.1 The ! prefix

Any line starting with ! is executed as a shell command if run from a code cell:

Example 1: Basic commands

!pwd
!whoami
!hostname

Example 2: Listing files

!ls -lh

Example 3: Creating directories

!mkdir test_directory
!ls -la

Example 4: File operations

!touch example.txt
!echo "Hello from Jupyter" > example.txt
!cat example.txt

Example 5: Combining multiple commands

!echo "File created on:" && date
Important notes about ! commands
  1. Each ! command runs in a new shell - variables and directory changes don’t persist between or code lines.
   # This WON'T work as expected:
   !cd test_directory
   !pwd  # You're still in the original directory!
  1. Capture output as a Python variable:
   files = !ls -la
   print(files)  # Now 'files' is a list of output lines

21.6.2 The %%bash magic command

The %%bash magic command allows you tell a code cell that it should interpret all of its content as bash commands and changes to persist between code lines.

Example:

%%bash
echo "Hello from Jupyter!"
ls -la
mkdir test_directory
cd test_directory
pwd    # This will show the path to the test_directory

21.7 Cell operations

21.7.1 Adding new cells

  • Click the + button in the toolbar
  • Or press Esc then A (insert cell Above)
  • Or press Esc then B (insert cell Below)

21.7.2 Deleting cells

  • Select the cell, press Esc then D, D (press D twice)
  • Or use Edit → Delete Cells

21.7.3 Moving cells

  • Use the up/down arrows in the toolbar
  • Or Esc then Ctrl+Shift+↑ or Ctrl+Shift+↓

21.7.4 Copying/pasting cells

  • Copy: Esc then C
  • Paste: Esc then V

21.8 Jupyter keyboard shortcuts

Jupyter has two modes:

21.8.1 Command mode (press Esc)

  • A - Insert cell above
  • B - Insert cell below
  • M - Change to Markdown cell
  • Y - Change to Code cell
  • D, D - Delete cell (press D twice)
  • Z - Undo cell deletion
  • Shift+Up/Down - Select multiple cells

21.8.2 Edit mode (press Enter)

  • Ctrl+Enter - Run cell
  • Shift+Enter - Run cell and select next
  • Alt+Enter - Run cell and insert below
  • Ctrl+S / Cmd+S - Save notebook
Pro tip

Press H in Command mode to see all keyboard shortcuts!

21.9 Shutting down Jupyter

When you’re finished:

  1. Save all notebooks (Ctrl+S / Cmd+S)
  2. Close notebook tabs in your browser
  3. Shut down the Jupyter server:
    • In the terminal where Jupyter is running, press Ctrl+C twice
    • Or go to the Jupyter home tab and click Quit
  4. Exit SSH connection:
   exit

22 Summary and Best Practices

22.1 Commands you’ve learned

Command Purpose Common Flags
whoami Display current username -
hostname Display server name -
pwd Print working directory -
ls List files -l, -a, -h, -t, -r
tree Show directory structure -d, -L
cd Change directory -
mkdir Create directory -p

mv Move or rename files -i
cp Copy files -r, -p, -i
rm Remove files/directories -r, -i, -f

unlink Remove symbolic link -

sort Sort lines -n, -r, -k
echo Print text -e, -n

man Manual pages -
\| (pipe) Chain commands -

22.2 Best Practices

  1. Always use tab completion - Start typing a filename and press Tab
  2. Use descriptive variable names - $REFERENCE_GENOME not $ref
  3. Comment your scripts - Future you will thank you!
  4. Test on small files first - Before processing huge datasets
  5. Use less for large files - Don’t cat gigabyte files!
  6. Keep a lab notebook - Document your commands and analyses
  7. Use version control - Git is your friend
  8. Validate your output - Check results make sense
  9. Document software versions - Ensures reproducibility
  10. Backup your data - Especially raw data!
  11. Protect raw data - Make it read-only with chmod -R u-w RAW_DATA/
  12. Use meaningful filenames - Include dates in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD)
  13. Check disk space - Use df -h before large operations
  14. Use symbolic links - Save space when dealing with large files
  15. Keep log files - Record all commands you run for reproducibility

22.3 Common Pitfalls to Avoid

  • Spaces in filenames - Use _ or - instead
  • Overwriting files - Be careful with > vs >>
  • Case sensitivity - File.txt and file.txt are different
  • Forgetting to check disk space - Use df -h
  • Not testing commands - Always test with -n or on small data first
  • Hardcoding paths - Use variables for flexibility

22.4 Text Editors Quick Reference

22.4.1 nano (easiest for beginners)

$ nano filename.txt
# Ctrl+O to save, Ctrl+X to exit

22.4.2 vim (powerful but steep learning curve)

$ vim filename.txt
# Press 'i' to insert, 'Esc' to exit insert mode
# ':wq' to save and quit, ':q!' to quit without saving

22.4.3 gedit (graphical, if available)

$ gedit filename.txt &

23 Appendix: Quick Reference Card

23.1 Essential Commands Cheat Sheet

# Navigation and information
whoami                      # Show current username
hostname                    # Show server name
pwd                         # Show current directory
ls -lah                     # List all files with details
tree -d -L 2                # Show directory structure (2 levels)
cd directory_name           # Change directory
cd ..                       # Go up one directory
cd ~                        # Go to home directory

# Getting help
man command                 # Read manual page
command --help              # Quick help
command -h                  # Short help (some commands)

# File operations
mkdir dir_name              # Create directory
mkdir -p path/to/dir        # Create nested directories
touch file.txt              # Create empty file
mv old.txt new.txt          # Rename file
mv file.txt folder/         # Move file
cp file.txt copy.txt        # Copy file
cp -r folder1/ folder2/     # Copy directory recursively
rm file.txt                 # Remove file
rm -r folder/               # Remove directory
rm -i file.txt              # Remove with confirmation (safer!)
ln -s target link           # Create symbolic link
unlink link                 # Remove symbolic link
cat file.txt                # Display file
head -n 20 file.txt         # Show first 20 lines
tail -n 20 file.txt         # Show last 20 lines
less file.txt               # View file interactively (q to quit)
wc -l file.txt              # Count lines

# File permissions
chmod u+w file.txt          # Add write permission
chmod u-w file.txt          # Remove write permission
chmod -R u-w folder/        # Recursive permission change
df -h                       # Check disk space
du -sh folder/              # Check directory size

# Download and compress
wget URL                    # Download file
wget -O name.txt URL        # Download with custom name
scp file.txt user@host:path # Copy file to server
scp user@host:file.txt .    # Copy file from server
gunzip file.gz              # Decompress
gunzip -k file.gz           # Decompress, keep original
tar -czvf out.tar.gz folder # Create compressed archive
tar -xzvf file.tar.gz       # Extract archive
tar -tzvf file.tar.gz       # List archive contents

# Text processing
grep "pattern" file.txt     # Search for pattern
grep "^>" file.fasta        # Lines starting with >
grep -v "^#" file.txt       # Exclude comment lines
grep -c "pattern" file.txt  # Count matches
cut -f1,3 file.tsv          # Extract columns 1 and 3
cut -d',' -f2 file.csv      # Extract column 2 (CSV)
paste file1 file2           # Merge files side-by-side
paste -d',' file1 file2     # Merge with comma delimiter

# Sorting and unique
sort file.txt               # Sort lines
sort -n file.txt            # Sort numerically
sort file.txt | uniq        # Remove adjacent duplicates
sort file.txt | uniq -c     # Count unique entries
cat file1 file2 > out.txt   # Combine files

# Variables and loops
VAR="value"                 # Set variable
echo $VAR                   # Use variable
for i in *.txt; do          # Loop over files
  command $i                # Process each file
done

# Pipes and redirection
command1 | command2         # Pipe output
head file | tail -1         # Get specific line
grep ">" file | wc -l       # Count matches
command > file.txt          # Write to file (overwrite)
command >> file.txt         # Append to file

# Useful utilities
echo "text"                 # Print text
echo -e "line1\nline2"      # Print with newlines
echo -e "col1\tcol2"        # Print with tabs
date +%Y-%m-%d              # Current date
date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S         # Timestamp

# Help and versions
command --help              # Get help
command --version           # Check version
